---
title: "SPI-M as a model for scientific advisory committees"
author: "Kath Sherratt"
date: today
format: html

### What was supposed to happen?

-   SPI-MO is called in response to national (Cabinet Office) emergencies, at which point it becomes a formal subcommittee of SAGE. The SPI-MO mandate is now to have two co-chairs (one academic, one policy), and voluntary contribution from academics who are recruited and invited by the co-chairs.
-   This arose from advisory groups of modellers (Imperial, Cambridge, Edinburgh) informally asked to support the response to 2001 foot and mouth disease.
    -   These groups and others were then formally called to support SAGE for 2009 H1N1 (Swine flu).
        -   A public Inquiry following this response (the Hine review) concluded in 2012.
        -   Notably, the Hine review recommended modelling should in future more clearly demarcate "evidence" from "advice"; and better integrate with SPI-B.
    -   SPI-M became a standing group attached to the Department of Health, maintaining a network of modellers and keeping preparedness models under review (e.g. the "sleeper research" protocol that supported development of the Cambridge/PHE model).
-   After 2009, SPI-M was operationalised in response to 2014 Ebola, 2016 Zika, and 2018 simulation Exercise Cygnet, before 2020-2022 Covid.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Potted history of SPI-MO

---UNEDITED: checked for sense but not sources ---

**2001: Foot and mouth disease**

The 2001 FMD outbreak was one of the first times mathematical models were used in real-time to directly inform disease control policy in the UK.
Three independent modelling groups (Imperial, Cambridge, Edinburgh) produced competing models that informed the controversial contiguous culling policy.
The experience was formative but also contentious: a [retrospective assessment](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspb.2008.0006) found significant disagreements between the models.
There was no formal advisory structure equivalent to SPI-M at this point -- modellers were brought in ad hoc.
The key lesson was that multiple models giving different answers required some mechanism for synthesis and arbitration.

**2009: H1N1 (swine flu)**

SPI-M-O was formally convened in 2009 for the H1N1 pandemic, as part of the SAGE advisory architecture.
This appears to be the first time SPI-M operated as a named, structured body ([Medley, 2022](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9525209/)).
It sat under SAGE alongside SPI-B (behaviour) and SPI-B&C (behaviour and communication).
The [independent review of the UK's swine flu response](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a7975f1ed915d0422068a10/the2009influenzapandemic-review.pdf) (the Hine Review) examined the advisory structures.
Notably, the Hine review recommended modelling should in future more clearly demarcate "evidence" from "advice"; and better integrate with SPI-B.
Between pandemics, SPI-M became a standing group attached to the Department of Health, maintaining a network of modellers and keeping preparedness models under review.
It published a [modelling summary for pandemic influenza](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/756738/SPI-M_modelling_summary_final.pdf) in 2018 that codified assumptions (e.g. 95% of cases over 9 weeks, 50% in a 3-week peak) used in subsequent planning exercises.

**2014: Ebola**

SAGE was activated for the West African Ebola outbreak, and [SPI-M-O was convened](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8165593/) alongside it.
However, there was a timing problem: COBR convened in July 2014 but SAGE was not activated until October, three months later.
A [Science and Technology Committee report](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm201516/cmselect/cmsctech/469/46906.htm) on "Science in emergencies: UK lessons from Ebola" examined this delay and the broader question of how quickly scientific advice could be mobilised.
Ebola also raised the question of SPI-M's scope: it was designed around pandemic influenza, but was being asked to advise on a very different pathogen and epidemiological context.

**2016: Zika**

A "Precautionary SAGE" (Pre-SAGE) was activated for Zika, a lighter-touch mechanism for assessing emerging threats when COBR had not been formally convened.
[SAGE minutes from the Zika response](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/sage-minutes-zika-outbreak-2016) are published.

**2016-2018: Exercise Cygnus**

[Exercise Cygnus](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-pandemic-preparedness/exercise-cygnus-report-accessible-report) (2016) was a Tier 1 national pandemic preparedness exercise simulating an influenza pandemic.
SPI-M modelling informed the scenario parameters (absenteeism levels of 30-35% based on SPI-M figures).
A notable finding was a "[lack of clarity about where modelling data could be accessed from for planning purposes](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/uk-pandemic-preparedness/exercise-cygnus-report-accessible-report)" -- i.e. local resilience forums didn't know how to get modelling support.
The 2018 [SPI-M modelling summary](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/756738/SPI-M_modelling_summary_final.pdf) was published after these exercises.

**2020-2022: COVID-19**

SPI-M-O was activated as a [formal sub-group of SAGE](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/scientific-advisory-group-for-emergencies/about) at the start of the pandemic.
This was its largest and most sustained activation.
As [Medley (2022)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9525209/) describes, SPI-M-O operated as a committee of independent academics working with a government secretariat.
Its main output was weekly consensus statements addressing questions from policymakers, "largely written by civil servants" but drawing on modelling contributions from members.
The R value and growth rate estimates became the group's signature product, published weekly and central to public communication.
Key developments during COVID: rapid expansion of membership; production of consensus statements at a pace and volume far beyond anything in previous activations; the "equal consensus" model where multiple independent analyses were synthesised; and growing tension between SPI-M's role as evidence synthesiser versus challenger of UKHSA's own analytical capacity.

**2025: Exercise Pegasus**

[Exercise Pegasus](https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/pandemic-preparedness-exercise-pegasus/) was a Tier 1 pandemic preparedness exercise led by DHSC with UKHSA, running September-November 2025 with core exercise days simulating emergence, containment, and mitigation phases.
Pegasus shifted back toward a "champion/challenge" model where UKHSA produces primary estimates for which the "consensus" process (implicitly) acted as peer review.
This created confusion about SPI-M's function: producer of analysis, describer of planned analysis, or peer reviewer of UKHSA analysis.
Note that the updated [SPI-M terms of reference (January 2025)](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/677feb016f01ae28ab5c0589/spi-m-terms-of-reference-january-2025.pdf) designate an executive chair from DHSC and a separate academic chair, formalising the dual accountability structure.
:::

## What actually happened?

-   Graham Medley summarises the SPI-MO consensus process as performing three functions: peer review; emphasis of uncertainty; shared responsibility.
    -   I think this works as a description of SPI-MO evidence production. However I think by taking the form of consensus, the functioning of SPI-MO in producing evidence took on a new form as political advice: peer review was perceived as quality assurance; emphasising uncertainty as risk assessment; shared responsibility as public legitimacy. I do not think the form and function were well matched.

## What happens next?

-   Institutional capacity for evaluation decays rapidly after an emergency. If not built in from the start, we cannot hope that it will happen retrospectively, or rely on 'natural selection' to express what we actually want from how modelling should interact with policy-making.
-   Key design questions for any new advisory structure follow directly from these three tensions.

Before we can adopt SPI-M as a model of scientific advice, I think we should clarify the following questions:

+------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+ \| Evaluation \| Evidentiary role \| Advisory role \| +============+==========================================================================================================================================================+=============================================================================+ \| Quality \| Peer review: Are the group reviewing each other equally (emphasis: real-time group dynamics), or reviewing a target (emphasis: long-term collaboration)?
\| Quality assurance: \| +------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+ \| Value \| \| +------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+ \| Trust \| \| \| +------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Uncertainty: \| Risk: Where does this group sit among the "three lines" of risk management?

Responsibility: What institutional support exists for members during and after the emergency?

Accountability:

::: {.callout collapse="true"}
### Why so little scientific evaluation of SPI-MO?

-   Protection: The UK COVID-19 Inquiry subsumed modelling into an exhaustive examination of governance, accountability, and process in a politico-legal framework; this diverted effort and effectively inhibited scientific evaluation or reflection.
-   Institutional memory: without institutional structures for supporting and retaining emergency responders, institutional memory is lost via burn-out and rapid career turnover, encouraged by the prevalence of short-term contracts in academia.
:::
